# How Solid-State Drives Wear Out Over Time

Solid-state drives (SSDs) degrade through a fundamentally different mechanism than hard disk drives. While HDDs suffer from mechanical failures—spinning motors, actuator arms, and head crashes—SSDs have no moving parts. Instead, their lifespan is consumed by the very act of writing data. Understanding this process requires a basic grasp of how NAND flash memory physically stores information.

## The Physics of Flash Memory

NAND flash stores data in floating-gate transistors, which trap electrons inside an insulated cell to represent bits. Writing data requires forcing electrons through an insulating oxide layer using a high voltage—a process called tunneling. Each write/erase cycle slightly damages this insulation. Over thousands of cycles, the oxide layer degrades until it can no longer reliably hold a charge, and the cell effectively dies. This is why SSD endurance is measured in program/erase (P/E) cycles, and why different flash types have different lifespans: SLC (one bit per cell) tolerates roughly 100,000 cycles, MLC around 3,000–10,000, TLC perhaps 1,000–3,000, and QLC even fewer, since packing more bits into each cell requires finer voltage discrimination and more precise (more stressful) programming.

## Write Amplification

The wear problem is compounded by how flash memory works at the structural level. Data cannot be overwritten in place; an entire block (typically containing many pages) must be erased before any page within it can be rewritten. To manage this, the drive's controller constantly shuffles data around, writing temporary copies and remapping logical addresses to different physical locations. As a result, the flash receives more writes than the host computer actually issues. # How Solid-State Drives Wear Out Over Time

Solid-state drives (SSDs) store data in NAND flash memory cells, and unlike mechanical hard drives, they have no moving parts to fail. Instead, their finite lifespan stems from a fundamental property of flash memory: each cell can only endure a limited number of write and erase cycles before it physically degrades. Understanding this process requires looking at how flash cells work, why they degrade, and how drive controllers manage the problem.

The root cause of SSD wear lies in the physics of a flash cell. Each cell is a transistor with a "floating gate" that traps electrons to represent data. Writing data requires forcing electrons through an insulating oxide layer using a high voltage (a process called tunneling), and erasing requires pulling them back out. Each cycle of forcing electrons through this insulator inflicts microscopic damage to the oxide. After thousands of these cycles, the insulation becomes leaky enough that the cell can no longer reliably hold a charge, and the data it stores becomes unreliable.

The severity of the problem depends heavily on the type of NAND flash used. Single-level cell (SLC) flash stores one bit per cell and can tolerate roughly 100,000 write cycles. Multi-level cell (MLC) stores two bits and endures perhaps 3,000–10,000 cycles, while triple-level cell (TLC) and quad-level cell (QLC) flash—common in consumer drives today—store three and four bits respectively, but tolerate only a few hundred to a few thousand cycles. More bits per cell means distinguishing between more voltage levels, which leaves less margin for error as the oxide degrades, so capacity and endurance trade off directly.

SSD controllers employ several clever techniques to stretch this limited endurance. **Wear leveling** distributes writes evenly across all cells so no single region burns out prematurely. **Overprovisioning** reserves spare capacity beyond the advertised size, giving the controller fresh cells to swap in
